sections.h: Paul's claim to be an apostle (1 Corinthians 9)
sections.b: Paul rests his standing on two things: he has seen the risen Lord, and the church at Corinth is the seal on his work (9:1-2). He claims the same rights as Peter and the Lord's brothers, including support from the churches and a wife who travels with him (9:4-6), and then explains why he has used none of them (9:12-18). Verse 9:5 also shows that other apostles, including Cephas, were married.

sections.h: Paul the free slave of all (1 Corinthians 9)
sections.b: Paul worked with his hands, took no pay from Corinth and said he had made himself everyone's slave to win more of them (9:6, 12, 19). He lived as a Jew among Jews and as one outside the law among Gentiles, though he was under Christ's law (9:20-21). Scholars discuss whether he kept the Torah himself while doing so or set it aside. His fear that he might be disqualified (9:27) shows he did not treat his own calling as secure without discipline.

sections.h: Paul the tentmaker and the worker's wages
sections.b: Paul and Barnabas supported themselves, while claiming the right not to (9:6, 12). He grounded that right in ordinary life (soldiers, vineyards, flocks), in the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4) and in a saying of Jesus (9:7-14). He chose to work in a trade, as he says elsewhere, to avoid being a burden (1 Thessalonians 2:9; Acts 18:3).

sections.h: Paul reads the law of Moses (1 Corinthians 9)
sections.b: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 25:4 (an ox must not be muzzled) and says it was written "for our sake" (9:9-10). He says he became like one under the law for those under the law, though not himself under it, and that he is not outside God's law but under Christ's law (9:20-21). Readers debate whether this means a Torah-observant Paul, a Paul who sets the law aside as his own rule, or one who keeps it as an adaptable custom.

sections.h: Games, markets and dinners in Corinth (1 Corinthians 9-11)
sections.b: The Isthmian Games, held near the city every two years, give Paul his picture of the runner and boxer (9:24-27). The meat market and the temple dining rooms lie behind the argument of chapter 10, and the dinners of wealthier households lie behind the trouble at the Lord's Supper (11:17-22). Together they show a church in a city of honor, patrons, clubs and sacrifice.

sections.h: Warnings to the confident (1 Corinthians 9:27; 10:1-13)
sections.b: Paul fears he could be disqualified (9:27) and tells the Corinthians that Israel, which had the cloud, the sea, the manna and the rock, still fell in the wilderness: "let the one who thinks he is standing take care that he does not fall" (10:12). He adds God's promise that no test will be beyond their strength and that a way out will be provided (10:13). The churches differ on what these warnings imply about whether a believer can be lost; the cards on 9:27 and 10:1-12 give each view.

sections.h: Married apostles (1 Corinthians 9:5)
sections.b: Paul says the other apostles, the Lord's brothers and Cephas take a believing wife along on their travels. This is one of the few direct pieces of evidence that Peter and other apostles were married. Clement of Alexandria, who defended marriage, read "a sister, a wife" as sisters who helped the apostles, and later writers used that kind of reading to fit a celibate clergy; the Reformers pointed to the verse to defend clergy marriage. Paul prefers his own single state (7:7-8) but does not require it of others.

sections.h: "Slave to all" as a metaphor (1 Corinthians 9:19)
sections.b: Paul says that although he is free from everyone he has made himself everyone's slave. The image reverses ordinary status in a Roman city and is Paul's way of describing a leader who serves. It is a metaphor for his own chosen service, not a comment on the institution of slavery, which he addresses at 7:21-23.

sections.h: Priests who eat from the altar (1 Corinthians 9:13)
sections.b: Paul reminds the Corinthians that those who serve in the temple eat from it and those who attend the altar share in what is offered (Numbers 18:8-32; Deuteronomy 18:1-5). He uses the priests' livelihood as a model for those who announce the good news. In chapter 10 the same principle works against idol temples: sharing the altar means sharing with the altar's god.

sections.h: Status and food in Corinth (1 Corinthians 9; 11)
sections.b: Paul refuses money from Corinth to avoid becoming a rich patron's client (9:12), and later rebukes the rich who eat their own supper while the poor go hungry at the Lord's Supper (11:21-22). In both cases wealth and status are tested by how they are used within the church.

sections.h: The wilderness as a pattern (1 Corinthians 10:1-11)
sections.b: Paul calls the events of the exodus and wilderness "examples" for the church (10:6, 11), using the cloud, the sea, the manna and the rock as signs and Israel's failures as warnings. The passage is a main New Testament example of reading the Old Testament typologically, and also of the claim that Christ was present in Israel's history (10:4).

sections.h: Fleeing idolatry (1 Corinthians 10)
sections.b: Paul says that an idol is nothing, but the sacrifices to idols are offered to demons, and that a believer cannot share the table of the Lord and the table of demons (10:19-21; compare 8:4). He draws on the golden calf (Exodus 32:6; 10:7) and the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:17, 21). The command is to run from idol worship (10:14), while meat in the market or at a private meal is not itself unclean (10:25-27).

sections.h: Paul's rules in 1 Corinthians 10
sections.b: Paul gives three rules. A believer must not take part in a meal at an idol's temple, because that is sharing the table of demons (10:14-22). Meat sold in the market may be eaten without asking questions (10:25-26). If a host serves meat at a private meal, one may eat it, unless someone points out that it was sacrificed; then one does not eat it, for the sake of that person's conscience (10:27-29). The aim is the good of others and the glory of God (10:23-33).

sections.h: The other person's conscience (1 Corinthians 10:25-29)
sections.b: Paul tells the strong to ask no questions because of conscience, and then says that if a person points out that the food was sacrificed they should not eat for the sake of the one who told them, and because of conscience (10:28), explaining that he means the other person's conscience, not their own (10:29). The passage shows that for Paul conscience judges one's own acts and also puts a claim on those who are free.

sections.h: Market meat and Psalm 24:1 (1 Corinthians 10:25-27)
sections.b: Paul tells Gentile Christians to eat anything sold in the meat market, giving as his reason Psalm 24:1: the earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord (10:26). This is not a statement about Leviticus 11; the issue is food associated with idols, not clean and unclean animals, though the two questions were close in the mind of a Jewish reader.

sections.h: "Our fathers" and "Israel according to the flesh" (1 Corinthians 10)
sections.b: Paul tells a mostly Gentile church that Israel in the wilderness is "our fathers" (10:1), speaks of "Israel according to the flesh" as a people with a priestly altar (10:18), and sorts the world into Jews, Greeks and "the church of God" (10:32). Readers differ on how far these phrases show the church taking over Israel's place, or Gentiles being added to Israel's story while Israel remains.

sections.h: Baptized into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:2)
sections.b: Paul says Israel was baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, a picture of baptism into Christ. Tertullian and other fathers read the passage as a foreshadowing of Christian baptism; Paul's use is a warning that the sign alone does not guarantee salvation (10:5-12).

sections.h: Spiritual food and the rock (1 Corinthians 10:3-4)
sections.b: Paul calls the manna and the water from the rock spiritual food and spiritual drink and says the rock was the Christ. Later readers heard the Lord's Supper in these words. Jewish traditions of a rock or well that followed Israel are a background.

sections.h: The wilderness generation as a warning (1 Corinthians 10:5-10)
sections.b: Paul lists five failures of the wilderness: craving, idolatry, sexual immorality, testing the Lord and grumbling, each with a mass death. The stories are Numbers 11, Exodus 32, Numbers 25, Numbers 21 and Numbers 16. The Corinthians are warned not to repeat them.
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 10:5-10; Numbers 11:4; Exodus 32:6; Numbers 25:1-9; Numbers 21:5-6; Numbers 16:41-49

sections.h: Twenty-three thousand in one day (1 Corinthians 10:8)
sections.b: Paul links the sexual immorality at Baal of Peor (Numbers 25) to the danger at Corinth's idol feasts, where eating, drinking and sex were often joined. His figure of 23,000 differs from Numbers 25:9 (24,000); the note on 10:8 gives the explanations.

sections.h: The Destroyer and the angels (1 Corinthians 10:10; 11:10)
sections.b: Paul names the Destroyer as the agent that struck Israel in the wilderness, a figure from the Passover story (Exodus 12:23). In 11:10 he says a woman should have authority on her head because of the angels, a phrase with many readings: guardians of order, fallen angels of Genesis 6, or witnesses to the church's worship.

sections.h: The ends of the ages (1 Corinthians 10:11)
sections.b: Paul says the warnings were written for us, on whom the ends of the ages have come. The church lives where the old age and the age to come overlap, after the Messiah's death and resurrection but before his return.

sections.h: Sharing in the body and blood (1 Corinthians 10:16-21)
sections.b: Paul asks whether the cup of blessing and the broken bread are not a sharing in the blood and in the body of Christ, and he adds that because there is one loaf, the many are one body (10:16-17). He compares this to Israel's altar and to idol tables to show that eating at a table makes one a partner of its host (10:18-21). Churches read sharing and body in different ways; see the card.

sections.h: The Supper at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:17-34)
sections.b: Paul calls the church's meal the Lord's Supper (11:20) and rebukes the rich for eating separately and the poor for going hungry. He reports the tradition he received about the night Jesus was handed over, the earliest written account of the Supper (11:23-26), with the bread for you, the cup as the new covenant, made in Jesus' blood, the command to remember and the promise of his coming. He warns that eating in an unworthy way and not discerning the body brought judgment, weakness, sickness and death, and tells them to examine themselves and wait for one another (11:27-34).

sections.h: The new covenant in the Supper (1 Corinthians 11:25)
sections.b: Paul quotes Jesus on the cup: the new covenant, made in his blood. The words take up Jeremiah's promise (Jeremiah 31:31-34) and the blood of Sinai (Exodus 24:8). Paul and Luke are the two writers who name the covenant new.

sections.h: Until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26)
sections.b: Paul says that each time the church eats and drinks, it announces the Lord's death until he comes. The same hope is in the cry Our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22), which the Didache puts at the end of its eucharistic prayers (Didache 10:6).

sections.h: Judgment as discipline (1 Corinthians 11:29-32)
sections.b: Paul says that sickness and death among the Corinthians followed their abuse of the Lord's Supper, and that being judged by the Lord is discipline so that they are not condemned with the world. Self-examination (11:28, 31) is the way to avoid it.

sections.h: Women who pray and prophesy (1 Corinthians 11:2-16)
sections.b: Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy aloud in the church's meeting (11:5) and asks only that they do so with their heads rightly covered. His arguments (headship, the order of creation, authority on her head, the angels, nature, custom) are debated, and so is the relation of this passage to 14:34-35. The churches' views are set out on the cards at 11:3 and 11:2-16.

sections.h: The passage in outline (1 Corinthians 11:2-16)
sections.b: Paul praises the church for keeping his traditions (11:2), says the head of every man is Christ, of a woman the man, and of Christ God (11:3), and argues that a man who prays or prophesies with something on his head, and a woman with her head uncovered, dishonors her head (11:4-6). He adds reasons from creation (11:7-9), authority on her head and the angels (11:10), mutual dependence in the Lord (11:11-12), nature (11:13-15) and the custom of the churches (11:16).

sections.h: Readings from Tertullian to today
sections.b: Tertullian (about AD 207) required veils for women and virgins; the medieval West wrote the rule into canon law (1917, canon 1262), and the 1983 Code dropped it. Calvin took the covering as the custom of a place. Conservative Anabaptist groups keep a prayer covering; some Pentecostal groups teach that long hair is the covering. Modern scholars argue that the issue in Corinth was hair, Roman religious custom, or the dress of respectable women.

sections.h: The image and glory of God (1 Corinthians 11:7)
sections.b: Paul says a man is the image and glory of God and the woman the glory of man. Genesis 1:27 says God made humankind, male and female, in his image, and readers have asked how Paul's statement fits. Most churches teach that men and women are both in God's image; the passage is read with Genesis 2 and with 11:11-12 in mind.

sections.h: The order of creation in Paul's argument (1 Corinthians 11:8-9, 12)
sections.b: Paul argues that woman came from man and for the sake of man (Genesis 2), then adds that man comes through woman and that everything is from God (11:12). Churches differ on whether the order of creation sets a lasting rule or serves an argument in a particular case.

sections.h: Prophesying in the assembly (1 Corinthians 11:4-5)
sections.b: Paul takes for granted that both men and women prophesy in the church's meeting. Prophecy is speaking God's word to build up the church (14:3). The passage is one of the New Testament's clearest signs that women did so.

sections.h: Freedom given up for others (1 Corinthians 9:1-23; 10:23-33)
sections.b: Paul says he is free, and then uses his freedom to make himself everyone's slave (9:1, 19). To the Corinthian slogan that everything is lawful he answers that not everything is helpful or builds up, and says that no one should look for his own good but the good of the other (10:23-24).

sections.h: Everything for God's glory (1 Corinthians 10:31)
sections.b: Paul ends the long answer about idol meat with a rule for all of life: whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do everything for the glory of God. His concern for what happens in the church's gathering (11:2-34) comes from the same rule.

sections.h: "The head of a woman is the man" (1 Corinthians 11:3)
sections.b: Paul writes that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God. The Greek word kephale ("head") is read as authority, as source or origin, or as prominence, and the note at 11:3 sets out the three readings and the choice between "man and woman" and "husband and wife." The order in the verse is not a straight ladder, and 11:11-12 qualifies it. Churches' teaching on ordination and on marriage is set out on the card at 11:3.
